topics.title: Quetzalcoatl: The Feathered Serpent

hook.text: Quetzalcoatl was a serpent covered in brilliant green feathers who gave humanity corn, writing, and the calendar.

buildup.text: He was one of the most important gods across all of Mesoamerica, worshipped for over two thousand years.

discovery.text: He traveled to the underworld and stole human bones, sprinkling his own blood on them to create a new human race.

twist.text: His rival Tezcatlipoca tricked him into getting drunk and committing a shameful act. Quetzalcoatl fled east in disgrace.

climax.text: He promised to return. When the Spanish arrived from the east, some believe the Aztecs mistook them for his return.

punchline.text: A god's broken promise may have helped end an empire.

quiz.question: What did Quetzalcoatl give to humanity according to Aztec mythology?
options: Gold, weapons, and fire
Corn, writing, and the calendar
Rain, thunder, and the ocean

topics.title: The Five Suns: Aztec Creation Story

hook.text: The Aztecs believed our world has been created and destroyed four times. We live in the fifth and final age.

buildup.text: Each previous sun was ruled by a different god and ended in a different catastrophe: jaguars, wind, fire, and flood.

discovery.text: The current Fifth Sun was born when a humble god threw himself into a bonfire and rose as the new sun.

twist.text: But the sun refused to move. The gods had to sacrifice themselves to set it in motion across the sky.

climax.text: The Aztecs believed human sacrifice kept the Fifth Sun alive. Without blood, the sun would stop and the world would end.

punchline.text: The Aztec universe ran on sacrifice, from the gods down to humans.

quiz.question: How was the Fifth Sun (current world) created in Aztec mythology?
options: Quetzalcoatl breathed life into a dark world
A humble god threw himself into a bonfire and rose as the sun
The gods carved the sun from a sacred mountain

topics.title: Tezcatlipoca: The Smoking Mirror

hook.text: Tezcatlipoca was the god of night, sorcery, and fate — an invisible force who could see all through his obsidian mirror.

buildup.text: He and Quetzalcoatl were eternal rivals, constantly creating and destroying each other's worlds in cosmic battles.

discovery.text: He could appear as a jaguar, a shadow, or the night wind. No one could hide from his all-seeing gaze.

twist.text: He was not purely evil. He tested humans to reveal their true nature, rewarding the strong and punishing the weak.

climax.text: His obsidian mirror was a real Aztec artifact — polished volcanic glass used by priests for divination and prophecy.

punchline.text: The god of darkness used a mirror to show people the truth about themselves.

quiz.question: What was Tezcatlipoca's obsidian mirror used for?
options: To blind enemies in battle with reflected sunlight
To see everything and perform divination and prophecy
To trap the souls of defeated gods inside it

topics.title: Huitzilopochtli: God of War and Sun

hook.text: Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed and immediately killed his 400 siblings to protect his mother.

buildup.text: His sister Coyolxauhqui plotted to murder their mother. Huitzilopochtli burst from the womb as a warrior to stop her.

discovery.text: He cut off Coyolxauhqui's head and threw it into the sky, where it became the moon.

twist.text: As the sun god, he fought the moon and stars every night. The Aztecs believed only blood could fuel his daily victory.

climax.text: The Great Temple of Tenochtitlan was built in his honor. Thousands were sacrificed there to keep the sun rising.

punchline.text: The Aztec capital was built to feed a god who was born fighting.

quiz.question: What happened to Coyolxauhqui when Huitzilopochtli defeated her?
options: She was banished to the underworld forever
Her head was thrown into the sky and became the moon
She was transformed into a river surrounding the temple

topics.title: Tlaloc: God of Rain and Lightning

hook.text: Tlaloc controlled all rain, floods, and droughts. Without his favor, the entire Aztec empire would starve.

buildup.text: He lived on a mountain surrounded by four jars. Each jar released different kinds of rain: good, bad, frost, and blight.

discovery.text: His paradise, Tlalocan, welcomed anyone killed by water, lightning, or disease — a lush green heaven of eternal spring.

twist.text: To please Tlaloc, the Aztecs sacrificed children. They believed the children's tears would summon the rains they needed.

climax.text: Tlaloc shared the Great Temple's summit with Huitzilopochtli — war and rain, the two forces that sustained an empire.

punchline.text: The Aztecs feared the rain god as much as the war god. Both demanded blood.

quiz.question: Why was Tlaloc so important to the Aztec empire?
options: He protected them from enemy invasions
He controlled all rain, and without it the empire would starve
He taught them how to build their capital city

topics.title: Mictlantecuhtli: Lord of the Dead

hook.text: Mictlantecuhtli was a skeleton god who ruled the deepest level of the Aztec underworld with his wife.

buildup.text: The dead had to journey through nine underworld levels, facing rivers of blood, clashing mountains, and icy winds.

discovery.text: Dogs guided souls through the underworld. That's why the Aztecs buried dogs with their dead to serve as spirit guides.

twist.text: Mictlantecuhtli tried to stop Quetzalcoatl from stealing human bones to create people. He failed, and humanity was born.

climax.text: His skull-faced image lives on in the Day of the Dead, where Mexicans honor ancestors with flowers and food.

punchline.text: The lord of the dead lost his bones, and we became alive because of it.

quiz.question: Why were dogs buried with the dead in Aztec tradition?
options: To protect the grave from robbers
Dogs were believed to guide souls through the nine levels of the underworld
Dogs were sacred to the war god Huitzilopochtli

topics.title: The Popol Vuh: Maya Creation Story

hook.text: The Popol Vuh tells how the Maya gods failed to make humans three times before finally getting it right with corn.

buildup.text: First they tried mud, but it dissolved. Then wood, but the wooden people had no souls and were destroyed by a flood.

discovery.text: Finally, the gods mixed corn with divine blood to create humans who could think, feel, and worship their creators.

twist.text: The corn people could see everything, like gods. Worried, the gods fogged their vision so humans could not see too far.

climax.text: The Popol Vuh survived the Spanish conquest hidden by Maya elders and was not published until the 1700s.

punchline.text: The Maya believed humans are made of corn — and in their diet, they were right.

quiz.question: What material did the Maya gods finally use to successfully create humans?
options: Clay mixed with river water
Corn mixed with divine blood
Stone carved from sacred mountains

topics.title: The Hero Twins: Journey to Xibalba

hook.text: Two brothers descended into the Maya underworld to play a ball game against the gods of death — and won.

buildup.text: Their father and uncle had gone before them and lost. The lords of Xibalba sacrificed them and hung a head on a tree.

discovery.text: The Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, were supernaturally clever, outsmarting every trap Xibalba threw at them.

twist.text: They let themselves be killed, ground into dust, and thrown into a river — then magically resurrected.

climax.text: They tricked the death lords into asking to be sacrificed too, then refused to revive them, defeating death itself.

punchline.text: They beat death by dying first and coming back.

quiz.question: How did the Hero Twins ultimately defeat the lords of Xibalba?
options: They won the ball game with supernatural strength
They tricked the lords into being sacrificed, then refused to revive them
They stole a magical weapon from the underworld throne

topics.title: Itzamna: The Supreme Maya God

hook.text: Itzamna was the creator god who invented writing, the calendar, and medicine for the Maya people.

buildup.text: He appeared as an elderly man with a large nose, wise and kind, ruling the heavens with quiet authority.

discovery.text: As lord of day and night, he controlled the cosmic cycles that the Maya used to build their famous calendar system.

twist.text: Unlike the violent Aztec gods, Itzamna was peaceful. He never demanded blood sacrifice, only reverence and wisdom.

climax.text: His gift of writing allowed the Maya to create the most advanced written language in pre-Columbian America.

punchline.text: The Maya's greatest god gave them something more powerful than weapons: words.

quiz.question: What gifts did Itzamna give the Maya people?
options: Fire, weapons, and a great wall to protect them
Writing, the calendar, and medicine
Corn, chocolate, and the secret of building pyramids

topics.title: Kukulkan: The Maya Feathered Serpent

hook.text: Twice a year, a shadow serpent slithers down the steps of a Maya pyramid — a trick designed a thousand years ago.

buildup.text: Kukulkan is the Maya version of Quetzalcoatl, a feathered serpent god of wind, rain, and learning.

discovery.text: The pyramid at Chichen Itza was built so that during equinox, triangular shadows create a serpent descending the stairs.

twist.text: This means Maya architects understood astronomy so precisely they could engineer a shadow play lasting 3,000 years.

climax.text: Thousands of tourists gather twice a year to watch the serpent shadow, making it one of the world's great spectacles.

punchline.text: A god made of shadows still appears at his temple on schedule, every year.

quiz.question: What happens at the Chichen Itza pyramid during the equinox?
options: The sun lights up a hidden chamber inside the pyramid
Triangular shadows create a serpent shape descending the stairs
A beam of light passes through a hole in the pyramid's apex

topics.title: Xibalba: The Maya Underworld

hook.text: Xibalba was a terrifying underground realm ruled by death gods who loved to trick and torment arriving souls.

buildup.text: To reach Xibalba, the dead crossed rivers of blood and pus, passed through houses of darkness, fire, and razor bats.

discovery.text: The lords of Xibalba included gods of disease, starvation, and fear — each representing a different way to die.

twist.text: Xibalba was not just mythological. The Maya believed natural caves were actual entrances to the underworld.

climax.text: Archaeologists have found ritual offerings deep inside caves, confirming the Maya truly believed they led to Xibalba.

punchline.text: The Maya underworld had a physical address, and people still visit it today.

quiz.question: What did the Maya believe about natural caves?
options: They were the homes of rain gods
They were actual physical entrances to the underworld Xibalba
They were sacred places where corn was first grown

topics.title: The Maya Calendar and 2012 Prophecy

hook.text: In 2012, millions feared the Maya calendar predicted the end of the world. It did not.

buildup.text: The Maya created three interlocking calendars tracking the sun, moon, Venus, and cycles spanning over 5,000 years.

discovery.text: Their Long Count calendar began in 3114 BCE and completed a major cycle on December 21, 2012.

twist.text: The Maya never predicted apocalypse. The 2012 date simply marked a new cycle — like a cosmic odometer rolling over.

climax.text: Modern Maya communities were frustrated by the hype, pointing out their living culture was being sensationalized.

punchline.text: The Maya predicted something about 2012: people would misunderstand their math.

quiz.question: What actually happened with the Maya calendar on December 21, 2012?
options: A major Long Count cycle ended and a new one began
The calendar ended permanently, predicting destruction
An ancient prophecy was fulfilled according to Maya elders

topics.title: The Ball Game: Sport of the Gods

hook.text: The Mesoamerican ball game was played for over 3,000 years, making it the longest continuously played sport in history.

buildup.text: Players used their hips to knock a heavy rubber ball through stone rings mounted high on the walls of a court.

discovery.text: The game represented the cosmic battle between the sun and underworld, light and darkness, life and death.

twist.text: In some versions, the losing team — or the winning captain — was sacrificed. Scholars still debate which team died.

climax.text: Over 1,500 ball courts have been found across Mesoamerica, from Honduras to Arizona.

punchline.text: The first organized sport in the Americas was also a death ritual.

quiz.question: What did the Mesoamerican ball game symbolize?
options: A competition for political leadership
The cosmic battle between the sun and the underworld
A harvest celebration held once a year

topics.title: The Legend of the Eagle and the Serpent

hook.text: Mexico's flag shows an eagle eating a snake on a cactus — an image from an Aztec myth about founding their capital.

buildup.text: The Aztecs wandered for 200 years, searching for the sign their god Huitzilopochtli promised would mark their homeland.

discovery.text: They found it on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco: an eagle on a cactus, devouring a serpent.

twist.text: That swampy island became Tenochtitlan, one of the largest cities in the world with over 200,000 people.

climax.text: Today it is Mexico City, built directly on top of the old Aztec capital, which sinks a little more each year.

punchline.text: A 500-year-old myth still flies on every Mexican flag in the world.

quiz.question: What city was built at the site where the Aztecs saw the eagle and serpent?
options: Chichen Itza
Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City
Tikal in the Maya lowlands

topics.title: Ce Acatl Topiltzin: The Priest-King

hook.text: Ce Acatl Topiltzin was a real Toltec king who became so legendary that he merged with the god Quetzalcoatl in myth.

buildup.text: He was a priest-king who banned human sacrifice and promoted art, astronomy, and peaceful worship of Quetzalcoatl.

discovery.text: His enemies — priests who profited from sacrifice — conspired against him and drove him into exile.

twist.text: As he left, he promised to return from the east. This prophecy echoed for five centuries until the Spanish arrived.

climax.text: Historians debate whether Aztecs truly believed Cortes was Quetzalcoatl returned, or if that story was invented later.

punchline.text: A peaceful king's exile created a prophecy that may have changed world history.

quiz.question: Why was Ce Acatl Topiltzin driven into exile?
options: He lost a battle against a neighboring kingdom
Priests who profited from human sacrifice conspired against him
He angered the gods by refusing to perform rituals

topics.title: The Weeping Woman: La Llorona

hook.text: La Llorona is the ghost of a woman who drowned her children and now wanders rivers wailing for eternity.

buildup.text: The most common version says she killed her children after her husband left her for another woman.

discovery.text: Some scholars trace La Llorona to the Aztec goddess Cihuacoatl, who wandered crying and carrying an empty cradle.

twist.text: The legend blends indigenous mythology with Spanish colonial stories, creating a hybrid that haunts Latin America.

climax.text: Parents still warn children to stay away from rivers at night, keeping a centuries-old myth alive as a safety lesson.

punchline.text: A myth born from heartbreak became Latin America's best bedtime warning.

quiz.question: What ancient Aztec figure may have inspired the La Llorona legend?
options: Coatlicue, the mother of the gods
Cihuacoatl, a goddess who wandered crying with an empty cradle
Xochiquetzal, the goddess of beauty and love

topics.title: The Chocolate Myth: Gift of the Gods

hook.text: Chocolate was considered so sacred in Mesoamerica that only gods, kings, and warriors were allowed to drink it.

buildup.text: Quetzalcoatl stole cacao from the gods and gave it to humans. It was consumed as a bitter, spicy ceremonial drink.

discovery.text: Cacao beans were used as currency. You could buy a rabbit for ten beans or a slave for a hundred.

twist.text: The word 'chocolate' comes from the Nahuatl word 'xocolatl.' Every chocolate bar traces back to Mesoamerican gods.

climax.text: The Spanish added sugar and took it to Europe, launching a global obsession worth over $130 billion today.

punchline.text: A god stole a bean, and now the whole world is addicted to it.

quiz.question: How was chocolate originally consumed in Mesoamerica?
options: As a sweet candy given to children
As a bitter, spicy ceremonial drink for elites
As a powder mixed into bread and pastries

topics.title: The Eagle and the Cactus: Founding of Mexico

hook.text: Mexico's flag shows an eagle on a cactus eating a snake. This image comes from an Aztec founding myth.

buildup.text: Huitzilopochtli told the Aztecs to wander until they found an eagle on a cactus. That would be their new homeland.

discovery.text: They found it on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco and built Tenochtitlan — now Mexico City — on that spot.

twist.text: Building a capital on a lake was genius: canals for transport, chinampas for farming, and natural defense.

climax.text: When the Spanish arrived, Tenochtitlan was larger than any city in Europe. A myth built an empire.

punchline.text: A bird on a cactus founded one of the greatest cities on earth.

quiz.question: What sign did the Aztecs seek to found their capital?
options: A jaguar drinking from a golden river
An eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake
A rainbow forming over a mountain peak

topics.title: Human Sacrifice: Why the Aztecs Killed

hook.text: The Aztecs sacrificed thousands of people because they genuinely believed the sun would die without human blood.

buildup.text: Their gods had sacrificed themselves to create the world. Humans owed a blood debt that could never be fully repaid.

discovery.text: Sacrifice was not cruelty for its own sake. It was the highest honor, and some victims volunteered willingly.

twist.text: The Spanish used sacrifice to justify conquest, but they burned people alive during the Inquisition at the same time.

climax.text: Modern scholars ask us to understand sacrifice within its own cultural logic, not judge it by outside standards alone.

punchline.text: Judging another culture requires understanding what they believed was at stake.

quiz.question: Why did the Aztecs perform human sacrifice?
options: To terrify neighboring civilizations into submission
They believed the gods sacrificed themselves to create the world, and humans owed a blood debt
Their priests invented it to maintain political power

topics.title: The Flower Wars: Sacred Battles

hook.text: The Aztecs fought Flower Wars — battles designed not to conquer but to capture living prisoners for sacrifice.

buildup.text: Both sides agreed to fight. Warriors sought to grab enemies alive, not kill them on the battlefield.

discovery.text: Being captured was considered an honorable fate. Sacrificial victims were treated with reverence before the ceremony.

twist.text: Flower Wars also served a political purpose: they kept vassal states weak and Aztec warriors constantly battle-ready.

climax.text: When the Spanish arrived, their Tlaxcalan enemies eagerly allied against the Aztecs — tired of being harvested.

punchline.text: The wars meant to feed the gods ended up starving the empire of allies.

quiz.question: What was the primary purpose of Flower Wars?
options: To expand the Aztec empire's borders
To capture living prisoners for ritual sacrifice
To settle trade disputes between neighboring cities

topics.title: Day of the Dead: Death Reborn

hook.text: Day of the Dead is not Halloween. It is a celebration where the living invite dead loved ones back for a visit.

buildup.text: Families build altars with photos, food, and marigold flowers to guide the dead back to the world of the living.

discovery.text: The tradition stretches back to Aztec rituals honoring Mictecacihuatl, the Lady of the Dead, over 3,000 years ago.

twist.text: Spanish priests tried to eliminate it. Instead, it absorbed Catholic elements and became even more powerful.

climax.text: UNESCO declared it an Intangible Cultural Heritage. Today it is celebrated globally, from Tokyo to Paris.

punchline.text: A 3,000-year-old death ritual became one of Earth's most joyful celebrations.

quiz.question: What ancient Aztec tradition gave rise to Day of the Dead?
options: Rituals honoring Huitzilopochtli, the war god
Rituals honoring Mictecacihuatl, the Lady of the Dead
Harvest festivals celebrating Tlaloc's rain

topics.title: Sacred Cenotes: Portals to the Gods

hook.text: The Maya threw gold, jade, and human offerings into cenotes — natural sinkholes they believed were portals to the gods.

buildup.text: Cenotes were the primary water source in the limestone Yucatan. Without them, no Maya city could survive.

discovery.text: The Sacred Cenote at Chichen Itza was dedicated to the rain god Chaac. Divers found thousands of artifacts inside.

twist.text: Offerings included gold from as far as Colombia and Panama, proving the Maya had continent-wide trade networks.

climax.text: Divers continue to find new artifacts, rewriting our understanding of Maya religion and trade with each discovery.

punchline.text: The Maya prayed by throwing treasures into holes that still reveal secrets.

quiz.question: Why were cenotes sacred to the Maya?
options: They were used as astronomical observatories
They were believed to be portals to the gods and were vital water sources
They contained magical herbs used in healing rituals

topics.title: Aztec Priests: Keepers of Cosmic Order

hook.text: Aztec priests lived atop pyramids, covered in dried blood, with matted hair that was never washed or cut.

buildup.text: They were the most educated people in Aztec society, mastering astronomy, medicine, writing, and ritual law.

discovery.text: Priests ran the schools, kept the calendar, predicted eclipses, and decided when crops should be planted and harvested.

twist.text: Despite their knowledge, they believed the universe needed constant blood to function — science and sacrifice coexisted.

climax.text: When the Spanish conquered the Aztecs, they destroyed the priesthood and burned nearly all their written knowledge.

punchline.text: A civilization's knowledge went up in smoke because conquerors feared it.

quiz.question: What happened to Aztec priestly knowledge after the Spanish conquest?
options: It was carefully preserved in Spanish libraries
The Spanish destroyed the priesthood and burned nearly all their texts
It was passed down orally and survives intact today

topics.title: The Sacred Ballgame: Sport of the Gods

hook.text: The Maya invented a sport where the losers were sometimes sacrificed. The ball court was a portal to the underworld.

buildup.text: Players used their hips, elbows, and knees to pass a heavy rubber ball through stone rings mounted high on walls.

discovery.text: The game re-enacted the Hero Twins' battle against the death gods. Every match was a myth played out in real time.

twist.text: Some scholars now believe it was the winners, not the losers, who were sacrificed — dying in glory was an honor.

climax.text: Over 1,500 ball courts have been found across Mesoamerica. The game lasted 3,000 years, outliving empires.

punchline.text: A rubber ball connected heaven, earth, and the underworld for millennia.

quiz.question: What did the Mesoamerican ballgame symbolically re-enact?
options: The creation of the sun and moon
The Hero Twins' battle against the death gods
The migration of the Aztec people

topics.title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan: Myth Meets History

hook.text: In 1521, one of the greatest cities on earth fell in 75 days. Mythology played a role in its destruction.

buildup.text: Tenochtitlan had 200,000 people, causeways, aqueducts, and markets larger than anything in Europe at the time.

discovery.text: Cortes had only 500 soldiers but allied with 200,000 indigenous enemies of the Aztecs who wanted revenge.

twist.text: Smallpox killed half the population before the final siege. Disease, not soldiers, was the real conqueror.

climax.text: The city was demolished. Mexico City was built on its ruins, and Aztec mythology nearly vanished with it.

punchline.text: A city of 200,000 was erased, and a new one was built on its bones.

quiz.question: What was the biggest factor in the fall of Tenochtitlan?
options: Superior Spanish weapons and armor
A combination of indigenous allies and smallpox devastating the population
Internal rebellion by Aztec citizens

topics.title: Codices: Books the Spanish Burned

hook.text: The Spanish burned thousands of Aztec and Maya books. Only about 20 Mesoamerican codices survive today.

buildup.text: Codices were folding books made from bark paper or deerskin, painted with mythological scenes and calendar records.

discovery.text: Bishop Diego de Landa burned every Maya book he could find, calling them superstition and lies of the devil.

twist.text: Landa felt guilty and wrote a book about Maya culture. Ironically, his book became the key to decoding their writing.

climax.text: The surviving codices are now among the most valuable documents in human history, studied in museums worldwide.

punchline.text: The man who destroyed Maya knowledge accidentally preserved enough to save it.

quiz.question: How did Bishop Diego de Landa accidentally help preserve Maya knowledge?
options: He secretly hid codices in a Spanish monastery
He wrote a book about Maya culture that became key to decoding their writing
He trained Maya scribes to rewrite their stories in Spanish

topics.title: Living Maya Communities Today

hook.text: Over six million Maya people are alive today, still speaking their languages and practicing ancient traditions.

buildup.text: They live across Guatemala, Mexico, Belize, and Honduras, keeping cultural practices despite centuries of colonization.

discovery.text: Maya ceremonies still honor the same gods from the Popol Vuh. Shamans use the ancient 260-day calendar for rituals.

twist.text: Outsiders treat Maya culture as a dead civilization. Living Maya are fighting to be seen as present, not past.

climax.text: Rigoberta Menchu, a Maya woman, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992 for advocating indigenous rights in Guatemala.

punchline.text: The Maya civilization never ended. Six million people are living proof.

quiz.question: How many Maya people are alive today?
options: A few hundred in remote areas
Over six million across several countries
The Maya civilization has no living descendants

topics.title: Mesoamerican Myths in Modern Mexico

hook.text: Mexico's national identity is built on Aztec mythology, from its flag to its murals to its national anthem.

buildup.text: Diego Rivera painted massive murals depicting Aztec gods and the conquest, making mythology visible in everyday life.

discovery.text: The Templo Mayor was discovered by accident in 1978 beneath downtown Mexico City, sparking a national obsession.

twist.text: Mexico embraces both its indigenous and Spanish heritage. Its identity is the collision of two mythological worlds.

climax.text: Corn, chile, and chocolate remain central to Mexican cuisine and culture — all gifts from Mesoamerican mythology.

punchline.text: Modern Mexico is what happens when ancient myths refuse to die.

quiz.question: What was discovered beneath downtown Mexico City in 1978?
options: An underground river system from the Aztec era
The Templo Mayor, the main Aztec temple of Tenochtitlan
A sealed tomb containing Aztec royal treasures

topics.title: Nahua Poetry: Songs from a Lost World

hook.text: Before the Spanish arrived, Aztec poets wrote verses about flowers, death, and whether life was just a dream.

buildup.text: Nahua poetry survived because a few priests recorded the songs in Latin script after the conquest.

discovery.text: Nezahualcoyotl, a warrior-king, wrote poems questioning existence — centuries before European existentialists.

twist.text: His most famous line asks: are we real, or do we only live in a dream? He wrote it in the 1400s.

climax.text: Today his face appears on Mexico's hundred-peso bill. A philosopher-king honored on currency.

punchline.text: A poet who questioned reality now lives on millions of banknotes.

quiz.question: Who was Nezahualcoyotl?
options: A Spanish priest who recorded Aztec songs
An Aztec warrior-king who wrote philosophical poetry
A Maya astronomer who predicted eclipses

topics.title: Why Mesoamerican Myths Still Matter

hook.text: Mesoamerican myths were nearly destroyed by conquest. Their survival is one of the great stories of cultural resilience.

buildup.text: They gave the world chocolate, corn, the concept of zero, and some of the most complex calendars ever created.

discovery.text: Their creation stories ask the same questions as Greek and Hindu myths: why are we here, and what do we owe?

twist.text: For centuries, Western education ignored these myths. Now universities worldwide are finally teaching them as equals.

climax.text: Understanding these myths means understanding the foundation of Latin American culture and over 500 million people.

punchline.text: The myths they tried to burn are now taught in the universities they built.

quiz.question: Why are Mesoamerican myths increasingly taught in universities worldwide?
options: They contain practical farming techniques still used today
They are foundational to understanding Latin American culture and 500 million people
They predicted modern scientific discoveries with perfect accuracy
